extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators and counsel practicing before the PTAB in IPRs
extracted.subtask_short: IPR motion to terminate on RPI grounds
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for evaluating motions to terminate inter partes review (IPR) proceedings based on alleged failures to identify real parties-in-interest (RPIs) and related defenses (e.g., whether a petitioner is a 'person' under Return Mail). Focused on PTAB practice and precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / waiver of issues
rubrics_metrics.description: A party should seek relief promptly after the need for relief is identified; delay in seeking relief may justify a denial of relief sought. A late action will be excused on a showing of good cause or upon a Board decision that consideration on the merits would be in the interests of justice. (37 C.F.R. § 42.25(b); 37 C.F.R. § 42.5(c)(3))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a Patent Owner fails to raise an issue (e.g., an RPI argument) in its Patent Owner Response when on notice that issues not raised may be deemed waived, the Board is likely to find waiver. Evidence that the underlying facts were publicly available before the response supports finding lack of diligence. Delay explanations (e.g., further research, client-counsel communication breakdown) are scrutinized; repeated or lengthy delay supports denial. Citations to prior PTAB decisions finding waiver are persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-cause / interest-of-justice standard for excusing late action
rubrics_metrics.description: Late actions may be excused only on a showing of good cause or if Board consideration on the merits is in the interests of justice (37 C.F.R. § 42.5(c)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Movants must show diligence or other strong justification; mere later discovery of publicly available materials or speculative claims of changed 'evidentiary landscape' (absent clear new evidence) will generally not suffice. The Board will examine when movant knew or should have known the facts and how promptly it acted thereafter.

rubrics_metrics.name: RPI requirement purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: The RPI requirement serves two related purposes: (1) to ensure that third parties with sufficiently close relationships to IPR petitioners will be bound by the outcome under § 315(e) (IPR estoppel); and (2) to protect patent owners from belated administrative attacks by related parties under § 315(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the significance of an unnamed RPI, evaluate whether adding the party would implicate time bars or estoppel concerns; if not, the RPI omission is less likely to require termination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to name an RPI does not automatically divest PTAB jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Our jurisdiction to consider a petition does not require a 'correct' identification of all RPIs in a petition (citing precedents such as SharkNinja Operating LLC v. iRobot Corp. and Lumentum Holdings, Inc. v. Capella Photonics, Inc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an RPI was unnamed, termination is not automatic—courts/panels consider whether adding the RPI would create time bar or estoppel issues. Precedent supports permitting correction or updating of notices where no prejudice (time bar/estoppel) results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy for failing to identify an RPI is not necessarily termination
rubrics_metrics.description: The remedy for failing to identify an RPI in a petition is not necessarily termination of the IPRs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether other remedies (e.g., updating mandatory notices, corrective steps) suffice, particularly where adding the RPI would not create § 315(b) time-bar or § 315(e) estoppel issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of public availability of supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If the evidence a movant relies upon was publicly available prior to filing of the Patent Owner Response (or the petition), that supports a finding that the movant could have timely raised the issue and thus undermines claims of newly discovered grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite dates of public reports, court opinions, and other exhibits; if exhibits predate the responsive filings, the Board will likely find a lack of diligence and waiver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board precedent: no need to consider unnamed RPI when addition would not create time bar/estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Precedent holds the Board need not consider whether an unnamed party is an RPI when the addition of that party would not create a time bar or estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315 (citing SharkNinja and related decisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis should focus on whether adding the RPI alters filing dates, triggers statutory bars, or changes estoppel exposure; absent such effects, the omission is less dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return Mail rule on 'person' and sovereigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Return Mail, a sovereign (the U.S. Government) is not a 'person' eligible to petition for post-issuance review; the Court applied a presumption that 'person' does not include the sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Return Mail's reasoning relied on factors unique to the U.S. Government; panels should be cautious about extending Return Mail to foreign sovereigns or political parties without persuasive reasons. The presence of a corporate petitioner (a 'person') that is allegedly controlled by a sovereign differs from the sovereign itself filing the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporations are 'persons' under the statute
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporations are 'person[s]' eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 311(a) to petition for IPR (citing 1 U.S.C. § 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where a corporation is alleged to be 'controlled by a sovereign,' the petition filed by the corporation remains one filed by a 'person' unless the corporation is disregarded via established veil-piercing or control doctrines supported by the facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to disregard corporate form (extensive control / fraud & injustice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The presumption of separate corporate form may be overcome in cases of extensive control or where separate treatment would result in fraud and injustice (citing First Nat’l City Bank v. Banco Para El Comercio Exterior de Cuba).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegations that a corporation should be treated as the sovereign require concrete, non-speculative evidence of pervasive control or misuse such that treating them as one entity is warranted. Speculative scenarios (e.g., state-sponsored industrial policy risk) are insufficient without record support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return Mail extension to foreign sovereigns requires persuasive justification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board will not extend Return Mail's holding to foreign governments or political parties absent persuasive reasons; Return Mail's analysis observes factors unique to the U.S. Government that may not apply to foreign sovereigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments to extend Return Mail must show why the unique concerns for the U.S. Government also apply to the foreign entity and why treating a corporate petitioner as the sovereign is justified by the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: RPI requirement also aids in identifying conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The RPI requirement assists Board members in identifying potential conflicts, but absence of an RPI identification does not itself establish a conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels should expressly consider conflicts but will not assume one merely from an alleged unnamed RPI; refer to Consolidated Trial Practice Guide and precedential PTAB decisions on conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Updating mandatory notices without loss of filing date when unnamed RPI was not time-barred
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an unnamed RPI was not subject to a time bar when the petition was filed, precedent permits parties to update their mandatory notices without loss of filing date (citing cases like Proppant Express Investments, LLC v. Oren Techs., LLC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the RPI was time-barred at filing; if not, permit corrective updates to notices rather than termination. Cite precedential practice and examples where filing dates were preserved after updating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder under 35 U.S.C. § 315(c) — joined parties may proceed independently
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 315(c), petitions by joined parties may be instituted on their merits and then joined to another IPR; termination of one petition (e.g., the lead petitioner) does not necessarily require termination of joined parties’ instituted petitions if those petitions were properly instituted and are not time-barred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When joined petitioners were separately instituted based on their own petitions and were not time-barred at filing, their IPRs can continue even if a related petition is terminated. Analyze each petition's filing/estoppel/time-bar posture separately.
